data.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
data.summary:
Input: root of a binary tree
Output: an integer representing the maximum path sum of any non-empty path
Rules: A path can start and end at any node in the tree and must contain at least one node. The path does not need to pass through the root.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 3 * 10^4].

data.approach: Post-order traversal with a global maximum tracker
data.key_insight: For any node, the maximum path sum that passes through it and continues upward is its own value plus the maximum of the max path sums of its left and right subtrees (ignoring negative sums). Simultaneously, the maximum path sum with this node as the highest point (turning point) is node.val + max(0, left_gain) + max(0, right_gain). We can track the global maximum across all nodes during a post-order traversal.

steps.title: Initialize global maximum
steps.detail: Set a nonlocal variable (or class attribute) to track the maximum path sum found so far, initialized to negative infinity.

steps.title: Define helper recursive function
steps.detail: Create a recursive function max_gain(node) that computes the maximum contribution of the current node to its parent path.

steps.title: Handle base case
steps.detail: If the node is None, its contribution is 0.

steps.title: Compute subtree gains
steps.detail: Recursively calculate the maximum gain from the left and right children. If a gain is negative, treat it as 0 since we can choose not to include that subtree.

steps.title: Update global maximum
steps.detail: Calculate the path sum passing through the current node as node.val + left_gain + right_gain and update the global maximum if this sum is larger.

steps.title: Return node contribution
steps.detail: Return the maximum gain the current node can provide to its parent, which is node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain).

data.overview: This algorithm uses a post-order depth-first search traversal to compute the maximum path sum in a binary tree. At each node, it calculates the maximum gain from the left and right subtrees, updates a global maximum path sum that can act as a turning point, and returns the maximum single-branch gain to the parent.
data.intuition: Imagine evaluating every possible junction in a water pipe network. At each junction, you calculate the best path coming up from the left branch and the right branch, combine them to see if it makes a record-breaking peak, and then pass only the single best downward path upward to your parent.

flow_nodes.label: Start maxPathSum
flow_nodes.detail: Initialize max_sum to negative infinity and define max_gain helper function.

flow_nodes.label: Check if node exists
flow_nodes.detail: If the node is null, return 0 gain.

flow_nodes.label: Compute child gains
flow_nodes.detail: Recursively compute left_gain and right_gain, ignoring negative values with max(0, ...).

flow_nodes.label: Update global max
flow_nodes.detail: Calculate current path sum through node and update max_sum if it's larger.

flow_nodes.label: Return max single branch
flow_nodes.detail: Return node.val plus the maximum of left_gain or right_gain to the caller.

flow_nodes.label: Return max_sum
flow_nodes.detail: Return the final global maximum path sum found.

pitfalls: Forgetting to ignore negative subtree gains using max(0, gain).
Returning the full split path sum to the parent instead of only the single best branch.
Failing to initialize max_sum to negative infinity, which causes issues with all-negative trees.

data.pattern_summary: Tree DFS involves visiting nodes recursively in a specific order (pre-order, in-order, or post-order) to accumulate information or compute values bottom-up from the leaves to the root. Reach for this when solving problems on binary trees that require combining results from subtrees.

pattern_options.name: Tree depth-first search
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to explore paths through the tree, combining information from left and right subtrees at each node.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers applies to linear structures like arrays or strings, not hierarchical tree structures.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window requires contiguous elements in a sequence, whereas tree paths can branch across left and right children.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While maps can store values, they do not provide the structural traversal needed to find paths across parent-child nodes in a tree.

signals.hint: Indicates the problem domain is a hierarchical tree structure rather than a flat array.

signals.phrase: maximum path sum of any non-empty path
signals.hint: Suggests we need to evaluate potential paths and keep track of the largest aggregate value.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach finds all nodes in the tree, iterates through every possible pair of nodes, computes the path sum between each pair while checking that it forms a valid simple path, and tracks the maximum sum found.
data.brute_force_why: There are O(n^2) pairs of nodes. For each pair, finding the paths from the root and calculating the sum takes O(n) time, resulting in cubic overall time.
data.bottleneck: Computing the path sum independently for every single pair of nodes by searching from the root repeatedly recalculates paths for overlapping subtrees.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times pathfinding functions are called inside the nested loops.
Notice that paths sharing common ancestors repeat the same tree traversals over and over.
Consider whether you actually need to test every pair of nodes from scratch, or if information from child nodes can be reused by their parents.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force solution repeatedly searches for paths between every pair of nodes, recomputing paths from the root from scratch. The optimized solution uses a post-order traversal to compute the maximum contribution of left and right subtrees in a single pass. At each node, it calculates the local path sum combining both children and updates a global maximum, returning only the single best branch gain to the parent.

derivation.note: Base case check runs for every node and its null children.
Recursively computes left gain, executing once per node.
Recursively computes right gain, executing once per node.
Combines current node value with left and right gains.
Updates the global maximum path sum.
Returns the maximum single-branch gain upward.

data.time_summary: Each node in the tree is visited exactly once during the post-order traversal. Lines 7 through 16 execute a constant number of operations per node. As shown by the measured evidence, when input size doubles from 16 to 32, step counts scale linearly from 134 to 262 (O(n)).
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(h), where h is the height of the binary tree, determined by the maximum call stack depth during recursion. In the worst case of a skewed tree, this is O(n), and in a balanced tree, it is O(log n).
data.takeaway: When a tree problem asks for paths that can turn at any node, compute sub-results recursively from the bottom up (post-order) and maintain a global variable for the peak value.
mistakes: Forgetting to discard negative branch gains using max(..., 0), which causes sub-optimal paths to reduce the total sum.
Returning the full split path sum up to the parent instead of returning only the single best branch gain.
Failing to declare nonlocal max_sum when updating the outer scope variable from inside the helper function.
